title: One day (109–115)
hook: better one day seeing how things arise and pass than a hundred years without seeing it

segments.voice: Yesterday, conquer yourself, and your line: the greatest conquest. Did you win one small inner fight, with one breath? Day one hundred eighty, the end of the thousands chapter.

Most of us have had one day we remember more clearly than whole years. A wedding. A birth. The day of a diagnosis. A day walking somewhere new, when everything, the light, the food, the faces, seemed to glow. And most of us have also had years that slid by and left almost nothing behind: the commute, the inbox, the same dinner. Length and life aren't the same thing. The last verses of chapter eight make that point six times over, and then name the one thing that makes a day worth more than a century. Today, verses one hundred nine to one hundred fifteen: one day.
screen: `ONE DAY YOU REMEMBER.` → `YEARS THAT LEFT NOTHING.` → `LENGTH ISN'T LIFE.`

segments.voice: The pattern goes like this. Verse one hundred ten, in Müller's English: someone may live a hundred years, careless and unrestrained, but “a life of one day is better if a man is virtuous and reflecting.” The next verses repeat the shape. A hundred years without wisdom, or one day with it. A hundred years idle and weak, or one day of real effort. And then verse one hundred thirteen: someone may live a hundred years without seeing how things begin and end, but “a life of one day is better if a man sees beginning and end.” Beginning and end. In Pali, udayabbaya: arising and passing away. In the Theravada tradition it sits at the center of insight practice: seeing, not just knowing, that every thought, feeling, sound and moment comes up and goes. The commentary tells this verse to a woman named Patacara. In a single terrible stretch, the story says, she lost her husband, both her children, her parents and her brother. She came to the Buddha out of her mind with grief, and he calmed her and taught her. Her own verses, preserved in the collection of the early nuns, describe the turning point: washing her feet, she watched the water run off, a short way, a little farther, then farther still, and saw in it how lives come and go. That same night, her verses say, her mind was freed. The last two verses of the chapter say the same of seeing the deathless and seeing the highest teaching. One day, seeing clearly, outweighs a hundred years of not seeing. Not because the years don't matter. Because a single day, lived awake, is where seeing happens.
screen: `A HUNDRED YEARS, OR ONE DAY.` · `UDAYABBAYA — ARISING AND PASSING.` · `PATACARA AND THE WATER.` · `WHERE SEEING HAPPENS.` · then, large: `ONE DAY, AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let's practice seeing beginning and end, at the smallest scale. Watch one breath begin, and end. Then the next. Listen for a sound: notice where it starts, and where it fades. Feel a sensation in the hands or feet: notice it arise, and change, and pass. Don't hold on to any of it. Just watch things come up and go, like water running off onto the ground. Everything you notice has a beginning and an end. The bell holds the time.
One day. Better one day seeing how things arise and pass away than a hundred years without seeing it.
Your line: one day, awake. Today, watch this one day closely. Notice three things begin and end: a conversation, a mood, a meal. Day one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: In insight meditation, practitioners watch sensations, sounds and thoughts arise and pass away, and the story of the nun Patacara is often told as an example of this seeing bringing freedom from grief.

fork.setup: you're Patacara, washing your feet. you pour water; it runs a short way, then farther, then farther still. what did she see?
options: how lives come and go, like the water.
that it was time to go home.
fork.reveal: in her verses, the water's short and long runs showed her how beings pass at every age, and her mind was freed.

original.note: Pali: arising and passing away, from verse one hundred thirteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'one day is better than a hundred years' means live fast.
what it means: one day of seeing things clearly as they arise and pass outweighs a lifetime of not seeing.
what a scholar hears: verse 113's 'apassam udayabbayam' names insight into arising and passing (udayabbaya-nana); Patacara's verses are Therigatha 112–116.
